title: How to Fix a Damp Basement: Test, Dry It and Stop the Smell
metaDescription: Fix a damp basement in 3 moves: a 48-hour plastic sheet test, humidity under 50% with a dehumidifier, and gutters and grading if the walls wick water.
h1: How to Fix a Damp Basement and Prevent Basement Dampness
keyword: how to fix a damp basement
keywords: how to fix damp basement walls
how to treat a damp basement
is it typical for basements to be damp
intro:
To fix a damp basement, first find out whether the moisture comes from humid air or from the ground: tape plastic to the wall for 48 hours and see which side gets wet. Humid air is fixed with a dehumidifier set to 45 to 50 percent and closed windows in summer; ground moisture is fixed with gutters, downspout extensions, grading and a masonry sealer.

Most damp basements are not leaking at all. They are humid, and the cool concrete pulls water out of the air the way a cold glass does on a summer day. This guide shows you how to tell the two causes apart, how to fix each one, how to get rid of the musty smell for good, and how to keep a basement dry enough to finish. It draws on EPA indoor humidity guidance, dehumidifier makers' instructions and standard basement moisture diagnostics.
quickAnswer: Run a plastic sheet test and buy an inexpensive hygrometer before buying anything else. If the room side of the plastic is wet or humidity reads above 60 percent, run a dehumidifier at 45 to 50 percent, keep windows shut on humid days and vent the dryer outdoors. If the wall side is wet, fix gutters and grading, then seal the walls.

sections.heading: How to Fix a Damp Basement: The Short Answer
sections.body:
**Short answer:** match the fix to the source. Basement dampness comes from two places: humid air condensing on cool concrete, and moisture wicking through the walls and floor from wet soil. Many basements have some of both. The clues you can see usually point to one of them.

| What you notice | Most likely source | First fix to try |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sweating cold-water pipes and ducts in summer | Humid air | Dehumidifier, pipe insulation |
| Musty smell, no visible water | Humidity feeding mildew | Dehumidifier, remove cardboard and old carpet |
| White chalky crust on walls | Water moving through masonry | Gutters, grading, wall sealer |
| Dark band along the bottom of walls | Wicking from wet soil | Downspout extensions, then coating |
| Damp rugs or carpet on the slab | Vapor through the slab or condensation | Test, then vapor-retarding underlayment or dehumidifier |
| Wet spots or puddles after rain | Seepage or a leak | Trace the path and waterproof |

Damp that peaks in July and August and disappears once the heat comes on is almost always condensation. If the damp shows up after storms or snowmelt, hugs the bottom of the walls or one side of the house, and leaves water marks, it is coming in from the soil.

If you see standing water, running water or a crack that drips, you are past damp and into leaking. Our step-by-step guide on [how to waterproof a basement](/how-to-waterproof-a-basement/) covers that work in order.

sections.heading: Is It Normal for a Basement to Be Damp?
sections.body:
Some dampness is common, but it is not something to live with. A basement sits in soil that holds water and stays near ground temperature all year, which in much of the US means 50s and low 60s Fahrenheit. That makes it the coolest, most humid part of the house in summer, and a natural place for moisture to collect.

### Why basements get damp
Warm air holds more water than cool air. When humid summer air drifts down the stairs or in through a window and cools by 10 or 15 degrees, its relative humidity climbs sharply. If it touches anything colder than its dew point, such as concrete, a cold-water pipe or a metal duct, water condenses on it. The same air that feels comfortable upstairs at 78 degrees becomes clammy at 64.

At the same time, concrete is porous. Soil moisture moves through block and poured walls and up through a slab, especially in older homes built without a vapor barrier under the floor. That moisture adds to the humidity in the room, which makes condensation worse.

### Why it is worth fixing
Dampness on its own is not dangerous, but it feeds mold, mildew and dust mites, which can aggravate allergies and asthma. Over years it can rot wood framing, rust appliances and ruin anything stored on the floor. Above all, it keeps the basement from being usable space. The good news is that most damp basements are fixed for a few hundred dollars and some patience.

sections.heading: Is the Dampness Coming From the Air or the Ground?
sections.body:
One cheap test answers this, and the answer decides everything else.

### The plastic sheet test
Cut a piece of clear plastic sheeting about 18 inches square. A square of aluminum foil works too. Clean a spot of bare wall and tape all four edges down with duct tape so no air can get underneath. Do another on the floor if the slab feels damp. Leave them for 24 to 48 hours, ideally in the weather when the dampness usually appears.

### How to read it
- **Water on the room side** of the plastic: the air is humid enough to condense on cool concrete. Start with humidity control.
- **Water underneath**, against the wall or floor: moisture is coming through the concrete from the soil. Start outside with drainage.
- **Water on both sides**: you have both problems, which is common. Fix the outside drainage and run a dehumidifier.

### Test more than one spot
Put squares on several walls: the north wall, the corner nearest a downspout, and the wall by the laundry. If only one wall shows moisture behind the plastic, you have a local water source outside, usually a short downspout or a low spot in the grading. That is a much smaller job than a whole-basement problem.

It is a home version of ASTM D4263, the plastic sheet check that flooring and coating crews run on concrete before they cover it. It is not a precise measurement, but it reliably answers the question that matters here.

sections.heading: What Humidity Should a Basement Be?
sections.body:
Keep a basement below 60 percent relative humidity, and ideally around 45 to 50 percent in summer. The EPA recommends indoor humidity below 60 percent and ideally between 30 and 50 percent to limit mold growth.

### Measure it instead of guessing
A basic digital hygrometer that shows temperature and humidity is one of the cheapest tools in the house. Put it near the center of the room, clear of the dryer, the sump and the dehumidifier's exhaust, and check it morning, afternoon and night for about a week. A basement that feels only slightly clammy often reads 65 to 75 percent on a summer afternoon.

| Reading | What it means | What to do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Under 50% | Dry enough for storage and finishing | Keep doing what you are doing |
| 50 to 60% | Borderline, mildew possible on cardboard and fabric | Run a dehumidifier in humid months |
| 60 to 70% | Mold and musty smell likely | Dehumidifier now, check moisture sources |
| Over 70% | Condensation on pipes, walls and stored items | Dehumidifier, plus look for water coming in |

### Do not overdo it
Driving a basement much below 45 percent wastes electricity, and very dry air in winter makes the rest of the house uncomfortable. In most climates the basement dries out on its own once the heating season starts, and the dehumidifier can be turned down or off.

sections.heading: How Do You Fix Condensation and High Humidity in a Basement?
sections.body:
If the plastic test showed water on the room side, these steps fix most basements.

### Run the right dehumidifier
Most damp basements in the 1,000 to 1,500 square foot range are well served by a dehumidifier rated somewhere from 35 to 50 pints a day on the Department of Energy's current test; size up for a larger or wetter space. Set it to 45 or 50 percent. Run a hose to a floor drain or choose a model with a built-in pump, so it keeps working without anyone emptying a bucket. Our guide to the [best dehumidifier for a basement](/best-dehumidifier-for-basement/) compares specific models and drain options.

### Keep the windows closed in humid weather
Opening windows to air out a musty basement feels right, but on a warm, humid day it pulls in moisture that condenses on the cooler concrete. Ventilate only on cool, dry days, or not at all. Through the summer, shut windows plus a running dehumidifier beat open windows every time.

### Remove the moisture sources
- Vent the clothes dryer outdoors through rigid or semi-rigid duct with tight joints.
- Do not hang laundry to dry in the basement.
- Put a sealed lid on the sump pit.
- Make sure furnace and air conditioner condensate lines drain properly.
- Wrap cold-water pipes in foam sleeves so they stop dripping.

### Warm up the cold surfaces
Condensation forms on the coldest surfaces first, usually the rim joists where the floor framing rests on the foundation and the top of the foundation walls. Seal and insulate those rim joists with cut-to-fit rigid foam or spray foam and you cut condensation there while saving on heating.

sections.heading: How Do You Fix Damp Basement Walls?
sections.body:
If the plastic test showed water behind the sheet, the soil outside is wet and moisture is wicking through the masonry. The fix starts outside, not with a can of sealer.

### Step 1: Send roof water away
Clean the gutters and extend every downspout so it empties at least 4 to 6 feet from the foundation onto ground that slopes away. One downspout dumping beside a wall is the single most common cause of one damp wall.

### Step 2: Fix the grading
The soil next to the house should drop away from the foundation, ideally about 6 inches over the first 10 feet. Fill low spots with compacted, clay-rich topsoil, not mulch or sand, and keep it several inches below the siding.

### Step 3: Wait and retest
Give it two or three heavy rains, then repeat the plastic test. Many damp walls dry noticeably once roof water stops soaking the soil against them.

### Step 4: Seal what is still damp
If dampness remains, scrub off the efflorescence and any loose paint, let the wall dry, and brush on a masonry waterproofer or apply a penetrating sealer. Our list of the [best basement wall sealers](/best-basement-wall-sealer/) explains which type suits which wall.

### Hollow block walls
Hollow concrete block holds water in its cores and wicks it through thin shells, so block walls often stay damp longer than poured walls. Fill visible holes, brush the first coat hard into every pore, and consider a product made for block from our [best cinder block sealer](/best-cinder-block-sealer-reviews/) guide. Water that collects in the cores and seeps out at the bottom course is a drainage problem, and may need weep holes into an interior drain.

sections.heading: Why Is the Bottom of the Basement Wall or Floor Damp?
sections.body:
Dampness at the foot of the wall and along the floor edge is one of the most common complaints, and it has a specific cause.

### The cove joint
The basement floor and walls were poured separately, so the seam where they meet is never fully bonded. When the soil around the footing is saturated, water rises through that seam and spreads across the floor edge. You often see a damp strip a few inches wide along one or more walls, worst after rain or snowmelt.

No wall paint or sealer stops water at the cove joint, because it is coming up from under the coating. The fixes, in order, are better roof drainage and grading outside, then an interior perimeter drain with a sump pump if water keeps coming. Our ranking of [basement waterproofing systems](/best-basement-waterproofing-systems/) covers those options.

### A damp floor in the middle of the room
A slab that feels cool and damp across the middle, or that darkens under rugs and boxes, is passing water vapor from the soil. Older slabs often have no vapor barrier underneath. A penetrating concrete sealer reduces vapor through bare concrete, and a vapor-retarding underlayment protects floating floors. If water actually pools, it is a drainage problem.

### Gravel or dirt floors
Some older basements and crawlspaces have gravel or bare earth floors that stay damp and musty. Cleaning them will not fix the smell. Lay a heavy polyethylene vapor barrier over the gravel, overlap and tape the seams, run it a few inches up the walls, and run a dehumidifier. A poured slab is the permanent fix.

### Painting a damp floor
Floor paint does not stop moisture. If you want a painted floor, prove the slab dry first and use a breathable product; our guide to the [best basement floor paint](/best-basement-floor-paint/) explains which paints tolerate below-grade slabs.

sections.heading: How Do You Get Rid of a Damp, Musty Smell in a Basement?
sections.body:
The musty smell is the gas mold and mildew give off as they grow. Dry the air and take away what the mold is feeding on, and the growth stalls; once it stalls, the smell fades. Air fresheners, charcoal bags and scented sprays only cover it.

### Step 1: Get the humidity down
Bring the relative humidity below 60 percent, ideally 45 to 50, and hold it there. Without this step the smell always comes back.

### Step 2: Find what is growing
Check the usual places: cardboard boxes on the floor, old carpet and padding, the back of paneling or drywall on outside walls, wooden shelves against concrete, ceiling tiles, the underside of the stairs, and the inside of an old dehumidifier bucket. Cardboard is a favorite food for mold, and replacing it with lidded plastic bins is one of the most effective changes you can make.

### Step 3: Clean small areas safely
EPA guidance says homeowners can generally clean mold on hard surfaces themselves when the total area is under about 10 square feet. Wear an N95 respirator, gloves and goggles, scrub with detergent and water or a suitable product from our [best mold remover](/best-mold-remover/) guide, and dry the area completely. Moldy drywall, ceiling tiles and carpet usually have to be removed. Never mix bleach with ammonia or other cleaners.

### Step 4: Clean the air while it dries out
A HEPA purifier with a real carbon filter catches airborne spores and absorbs odor while the space dries. Our guide to the [best air purifier for mold](/best-air-purifier-for-mold/) explains why carbon weight matters for musty smells.

### When to call a professional
Bring in a qualified remediation contractor for growth larger than about 10 square feet, mold inside walls or ductwork, mold that keeps returning after cleaning, or anyone in the house with asthma or a weakened immune system.

sections.heading: Does Sunlight or Airing Out Help a Damp Basement?
sections.body:
Sunlight helps a little; airing out often hurts.

### Sunlight
Sun through a basement window warms the surfaces it hits and dries them slightly, and ultraviolet light does slow mold growth on directly lit surfaces. But basement windows are small and sit low, so the effect is limited to a few square feet near the window. Sunlight will not dry a block wall, a slab or the air in a closed room. On the outside, though, sun is valuable: trimming shrubs and trees so the soil along the foundation gets sun and air helps it dry between storms.

### Opening windows
Ventilation helps only when the outdoor air is drier than the basement air. On a cool, dry day in spring or fall, opening windows and running a fan can flush out moisture and odor. On a warm, humid summer day, it does the opposite: humid outdoor air cools as it enters, its relative humidity rises, and it condenses on the concrete.

### A simple rule
Compare the outdoor dew point with the basement temperature. If the outdoor dew point is well below the basement air temperature, ventilating is safe. If it is close to or above it, keep the windows shut and let the dehumidifier work. A hygrometer in the basement and a weather app showing dew point make this an easy daily check.

sections.heading: How Do You Prepare a Damp Basement to Be Finished?
sections.body:
You can finish a basement that used to be damp, but only after it has proved it stays dry.

### Prove it first
You want a year, or at least a whole wet season, of hygrometer readings in the low 50s or below, with no fresh white crust, water marks or damp patches after heavy rain. Finishing before that hides the evidence you need to judge whether your fixes worked.

### Design the walls for occasional moisture
Building science guidance generally favors rigid foam insulation glued directly to the concrete with taped seams, rather than fiberglass batts behind a plastic sheet. Plastic against a cold wall can trap moisture and grow mold behind the drywall. Use pressure-treated lumber for bottom plates that touch concrete and leave a small gap at the bottom of the drywall.

### Choose flooring that tolerates damp
Good options include vinyl plank or tile with a waterproof core, ceramic or porcelain tile, and concrete that has been sealed or painted. Our guide to [vinyl plank flooring](/best-vinyl-plank-flooring/) covers basement-friendly options. Wall-to-wall carpet over a pad is the worst choice, because it traps water and feeds mold before you notice.

### Store things as if it might get damp again
Swap cardboard boxes for bins with lids, lift everything off the slab on wire or plastic shelves, and pull the shelves a few inches out from the outside walls so air can get behind them. Keep the dehumidifier in the finished plan, with a permanent drain line.

sections.heading: How Do You Prevent Basement Dampness Year-Round?
sections.body:
Preventing basement dampness is mostly a seasonal routine. A few checks each season keep a dry basement dry.

### Spring
Clean gutters once trees have dropped their seeds and flowers. Reattach downspout extensions knocked loose over winter, and check the soil slope once the ground thaws. Pour water into the sump pit to test the pump. Walk the basement after the first big spring rains and look for new damp spots.

### Summer
This is condensation season. Run the dehumidifier at 45 to 50 percent, keep windows shut on humid days, and clean the dehumidifier filter every few weeks. Make sure the drain hose is clear and the unit actually cycles; a full bucket or iced coils mean it is doing nothing.

### Fall
Clean the gutters again after the leaves drop. This is the most important cleaning of the year. Check window well covers and clear leaves out of the wells. As heating starts, turn the dehumidifier down.

### Winter
Keep snow piles away from the foundation where possible, and make sure the sump discharge line is not frozen or buried. Watch for condensation on windows upstairs, a sign that indoor humidity from cooking and showers is higher than it should be.

Keep a short log of hygrometer readings and anything you notice. After one year, the patterns are obvious, and you will know exactly which fix is doing the work.

mistakes.title: Opening windows on humid summer days
mistakes.body: Airing out a musty basement feels like the right move, but warm, humid air condenses on cool concrete and makes the dampness worse. Ventilate only when the outdoor air is cool and dry, and keep the basement closed with a dehumidifier running through summer. A hygrometer shows the difference within a day.

mistakes.title: Sealing walls that are only sweating
mistakes.body: If the plastic sheet test shows water on the room side, the wall is not leaking; humid air is condensing on it. A masonry sealer does nothing for that and wastes a weekend and the cost of the product. Dehumidify first, and coat only the walls that show moisture behind the plastic.

mistakes.title: Expecting a dehumidifier to fix wet walls
mistakes.body: A dehumidifier dries the air but does nothing about water wicking through walls from saturated soil. If downspouts empty beside the foundation, the machine runs nonstop and the walls stay damp. Fix the gutters, downspouts and grading, then let the dehumidifier handle what is left.

mistakes.title: Storing cardboard boxes on the floor
mistakes.body: Cardboard soaks up moisture from concrete and feeds mold, which is often the hidden source of a stubborn musty smell. Repack into plastic bins with lids, put them on shelving rather than the floor, and leave space between the shelves and the foundation walls.

mistakes.title: Finishing the basement before proving it dry
mistakes.body: Drywall and carpet hide moisture and feed mold, and tearing them out later costs far more than waiting. Track the humidity and check for damp spots for a full year after your fixes, then finish with rigid foam against the concrete, pressure-treated plates and moisture-tolerant flooring.

faqs.q: How do you fix a damp basement?
faqs.a: Find the source first with a 48-hour plastic sheet test. If the room side of the plastic gets wet, the problem is humid air: run a dehumidifier at 45 to 50 percent, keep windows shut on humid days, vent the dryer outdoors and insulate cold pipes. If the wall side gets wet, moisture is coming from the soil: fix gutters, downspouts and grading, then seal the walls.

faqs.q: Is it typical for basements to be damp?
faqs.a: Yes, some dampness is common because basements sit in moist soil and stay cool, so humid summer air condenses on the concrete. Common does not mean harmless. Humidity above about 60 percent feeds mold, mildew and dust mites and can damage stored items and wood. Most damp basements are fixed with a dehumidifier and better roof drainage.

faqs.q: What can I use to get the damp smell out of my basement?
faqs.a: Lower the humidity first, because the smell comes from mold and mildew that grow above about 60 percent. Run a dehumidifier set to 45 to 50 percent, remove cardboard, old carpet and anything moldy, and clean small hard-surface patches with detergent or a mold cleaner. A HEPA air purifier with a heavy carbon filter helps clear the remaining odor.

faqs.q: Why does my basement smell musty when it looks dry?
faqs.a: Mold and mildew can grow on dust, cardboard, wood and fabric whenever humidity stays above roughly 60 percent, even with no visible water. The musty odor is the gas they release. Check the humidity with a hygrometer. If it is high, a dehumidifier and removing stored cardboard and old carpet usually clear the smell within a few weeks.

faqs.q: How do you fix damp basement walls from the inside?
faqs.a: Confirm with a plastic sheet test that the moisture comes through the wall, then fix outside drainage first, since interior fixes work better with less water behind them. Inside, scrub off efflorescence and loose paint, let the wall dry, and brush on two coats of masonry waterproofer or apply a penetrating sealer. Run a dehumidifier to handle remaining humidity.

faqs.q: What humidity should a basement be?
faqs.a: Keep a basement below 60 percent relative humidity, and aim for 45 to 50 percent in summer. The EPA recommends indoor humidity below 60 percent and ideally 30 to 50 percent to limit mold. Going much below 45 percent mostly wastes electricity. An inexpensive digital hygrometer tells you where you stand.

faqs.q: How long does it take to dry out a damp basement?
faqs.a: The air dries quickly: with the right-size dehumidifier and the outside water problems handled, most basements hit their humidity target in somewhere between a few days and two weeks. Concrete walls and slabs hold moisture much longer and often take a full season to dry out. Judge success over several months with a hygrometer and by watching for new efflorescence or damp spots.

bottomLine: Fixing a damp basement starts with two cheap tools: a sheet of plastic and a hygrometer. If the plastic fogs on the room side, your enemy is humid air: keep summer windows shut, set a dehumidifier to 45 to 50 percent, send the dryer exhaust outdoors and wrap cold pipes. Water on the wall side means wet soil, so fix the gutters, downspouts and grading before sealing the walls. Clear out cardboard and old carpet, clean small mold patches safely, keep up a simple seasonal routine, and give the basement a full year of dry readings before you finish it.
